title: Newspapers and television
subtitle: daily, headline, documentary, channel
summary: Describe newspapers and the things in them, name the main types of TV programme, and report what you read or heard.

lesson.heading: Newspapers
lesson.text: Most **papers** (newspapers) are **daily**, which means they **come out** - appear in the shops - every day. Another way to say this is that they **are published**. Some papers are **national**, for the whole country; others are **regional**, for one part of it. Magazines are usually **weekly** or **monthly**.

examples.text: The Times is a **national daily** paper. It **comes out** every morning.
We take a **regional** paper for news about the south-west.
The magazine is **published monthly**, so there are twelve numbers a year.

lesson.note: Newspapers published on the Internet are called **e-papers**. A **mobile edition** is a newspaper you read on your phone.

lesson.heading: What you find in a newspaper
rows: a piece of writing about a news item, written by a reporter or journalist
a piece of writing about an important subject, e.g. an article on drugs
the title in large letters above a report, e.g. GOVERNMENT LOSES VOTE
a piece of writing giving an opinion, e.g. a review of a new book or film
words and pictures about a product, to make people buy it
lesson.note: We say a report **on** or **about** a crime, and an advert **for** shampoo.

lesson.heading: Television
lesson.text: If you **broadcast** something, you send it out on TV, radio or the Internet. There are many **broadcasting companies** and many **programmes**. Famous people who appear on TV are **celebrities**, and something everybody knows about is **well known**.

examples.text: The match will be **broadcast** live on Saturday evening.
**Well-known** examples of reality TV are Pop Idol and The X Factor.
*A:* Are they mostly famous people? *B:* Yes, they're all **celebrities**.

lesson.heading: Types of TV programme
rows: a description of what the weather will be like in the next few days
a programme that gives facts about real situations and real people
a programme where famous people are asked questions about themselves
a number of programmes with the same characters or the same subject
a regular series, often two or three times a week, about a group of people who live in the same area
a programme which follows ordinary people or celebrities through situations or challenges

left.label: channel - for television
examples: How many **channels** do you get on your TV?

right.label: station - for radio
examples: *A:* What **station** are you listening to? *B:* Radio 1 - it's mostly pop music.
Rock FM is the name of a radio **station**.

lesson.heading: Reporting what you read or heard
lesson.text: When you say where your information came from, use **It says in ...** or **According to ...**. News is also reported online through **podcasts** - radio programmes you download and play on your computer or phone - and many papers have online **forums** where readers leave messages.

examples.text: **It said in** The Times that the plane crashed in the sea.
examples.wrong: It was written in The Times

examples.text: **According to** the news on TV last night, the plane crashed in the sea.
Have you heard the latest business **podcast** on the CNN website?

lesson.text: We say *It says in the paper ...* or *According to the paper ...* - never ~~It's written in the paper~~.

exercises.prompt: Rock FM is the name of a radio ___.
exercises.explanation: We use station for radio and channel for television.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is NOT a type of TV programme?
exercises.explanation: A headline is the title above a report in a newspaper, not a TV programme.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.right: a factual programme about real people and situations
a programme that interviews famous people
programmes several times a week about the same people
a piece of writing giving an opinion about a film or book

exercises.prompt: *A:* Can we watch the news now? *B:* Yes, it's on ___ Four.
exercises.explanation: Television broadcasting uses channel; radio uses station.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Is it a national paper? *B:* No, it's a ___ paper for the south-west.
exercises.explanation: A national paper is for the whole country; a regional paper is for one part of it.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Is the magazine published every day? *B:* No, it ___ monthly.
exercises.explanation: A paper or magazine comes out (= is published) daily, weekly or monthly.

exercises.prompt: Is it a TV programme or something you find in a newspaper?
Do you understand this ___? '200 WOMEN GIVEN WRONG DIAGNOSIS'
exercises.explanation: A headline is the title written in large letters above a report.

exercises.prompt: The manager was interviewed for the paper by one of their well-known ___.
exercises.explanation: Reports in a paper are written by reporters or journalists.

exercises.prompt: You often see ___ in the paper which promise that you can learn a language in ten hours. It isn't true.
exercises.explanation: Adverts (advertisements) try to make people buy a product.

exercises.prompt: ___ to the weather forecast last night, it's going to rain today.
exercises.explanation: We use According to ... to say where our information came from.

exercises.statement: It's written in the paper that the interest rate is likely to go up soon.
exercises.explanation: It says in the paper that the interest rate is likely to go up soon. We do not say 'It's written in the paper'.

exercises.prompt: Report the news you read in the newspaper.
exercises.answer: It says in the paper that the plane crashed
exercises.explanation: It says in the paper that ... is the normal way to report what you have read.
